name: Selective perception
statement: People given the same complex event pick out the parts that suit their allegiance or their job, and report back a different event from the one their neighbour reports.
meaning: The name is a label over three literatures that share a premise and little else. The first is the New Look work of the 1940s and 1950s on perceptual defence, which measured how long a word had to be shown before a viewer could read it. The second is social perception, where partisans watch one event and describe two. The third is organisational, where a manager reads a business case and names the problem belonging to his own department. Dearborn and Simon give the shared premise in one line: the more complex or ambiguous the stimulus, the more the perception is determined by what is already in the subject and the less by what is in the stimulus. They take that formulation from Bruner's paper on perceptual readiness. Nothing in the label fixes where the selection happens. It might be in what the eye goes to, in what gets stored, or in what a person says a week later, and the classic studies were not built to tell those apart. The one modern study that measured all three stages on the same viewers found the difference only in the last.

origin.who: DeWitt C. Dearborn and Herbert A. Simon
origin.note: A five-page note that put the term on the phenomenon in the form management and popular writing still use. The demonstration everyone cites is four years older and does not use the term: Hastorf and Cantril's study of a football game appeared in 1954.

evidence: Hastorf and Cantril studied the Dartmouth against Princeton game of 23 November 1951 at Palmer Stadium. Princeton won, and the official statistics recorded 70 penalty yards against Dartmouth and 25 against Princeton. A week later they gave a questionnaire to psychology students at both colleges, 163 at Dartmouth and 161 at Princeton. Of the Princeton students 93 percent called the game rough and dirty and none called it clean and fair. Among Dartmouth students 42 percent said rough and dirty and 13 percent clean and fair, while 39 percent wrote in a category of their own, rough and fair. Asked who started the rough play, 86 percent of Princeton students blamed Dartmouth, against 36 percent of Dartmouth students. Then a film of the game was shown to two Dartmouth fraternities on 7 December and to two Princeton undergraduate clubs early in January. Watching it, 48 Dartmouth students marked a mean of 4.3 infractions by Dartmouth and 4.4 by Princeton. The 49 Princeton students marked 9.8 by Dartmouth and 4.2 by Princeton. The paper reports one test, a footnote to the table saying the Dartmouth-team counts differ at the .01 level. Dearborn and Simon gave 23 middle managers from one manufacturing firm a 10,000-word teaching case about the Castengo Steel Company and asked each to write down the most important problem a new president should tackle first. Five of the six sales executives named sales, against five of the other 17, which the authors report as 83 percent against 29 percent and significant at the 5 percent level. Four of the five production executives named organisation, 80 percent against 22 percent, again at the 5 percent level. Three of the four accounting executives named sales too, and the authors fold them in with sales to reach eight of ten against two of the remaining 13. No test statistic is printed for either comparison.

replication.headline: Rival fans still report different games, d = 0.83 among 58 supporters of the 2013 Champions League final, and the eye movements and recall of those same fans did not differ at all.
replication.detail: Huff and colleagues recruited 132 applicants and invited the 58 keenest, 33 Borussia Dortmund fans and 25 Bayern Munich fans, to watch the live broadcast in separate cubicles. Ten to twelve days later they rated how much each team had contributed in possession, tackles won and scoring chances. Bayern fans rated Bayern's contribution higher than Dortmund fans did, t(49) = 2.89, p = 0.006, d = 0.83. The earlier stages gave nothing. Gaze coherence with one's own fan group minus coherence with the other group came to M = -0.03, SD = 0.27, t(14) = -0.46, p = 0.655, with a Bayes factor of 5.15 favouring the null. Event segmentation agreement gave t(33) = -1.49, p = 0.144, and a Bayes factor of 12.50 for the null. Cued recall showed no effect of fandom immediately or at the delayed test. Boon and Davies had run a modernised version of the football design in 1996. Their abstract reports that perceptions were still distorted towards the preferred team, that participants did not know it, and that they justified the distortion afterwards. Their article was not obtained. The management strand went the other way. Walsh gave a shorter case to 121 midcareer managers and measured their belief structures by card sort. Three of his four hypotheses failed: work history did not predict belief-structure content, information use did not vary by group, and a targeted test of Dearborn and Simon's own domains of human relations, accounting and marketing was not significant. Managers named 7.12 problems each on average and used 25.09 pieces of case information. Beyer and five co-authors then ran a systematic replication of both studies. Their abstract reports that the two sets of conclusions differ because the procedures differ, and that managers perceive more broadly when encouraged to name more problems. It adds that functional experience can produce selective imperception as well as selective perception. That article is paywalled and only the abstract was read.

study.cite: Huff, M., Papenmeier, F., Maurer, A. E., Meitz, T. G. K., Garsoffky, B., & Schwan, S. (2017). Fandom biases retrospective judgments not perception. Scientific Reports, 7, 43083.

limits: Both famous studies are small and neither reports an effect size. Hastorf and Cantril tested the film on 48 and 49 students drawn from two fraternities and two undergraduate clubs, shown a month apart. Their own footnote warns that a film of a football game follows the ball and omits much of the action. Dearborn and Simon had 23 people from one company, and only 10 of the 23 named sales at all. The perceptual defence strand is the weakest of the three here. McGinnies published the recognition-threshold result in 1949, Howes and Solomon published a critical note in 1950 and McGinnies replied in the next six pages; none of those three papers was obtained for this entry. What was obtained is a 1984 repetition by York, Mandour and Jex, whose abstract reports that taboo words again had higher thresholds than neutral words while the skin-conductance difference did not come out. The modern experimental base is thin. Searching Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC and the works citing Hastorf and Cantril since 2010 turned up one study that separates perception from judgement, and it runs on 58 people with the eye-tracking arm down to 15. Beyer and colleagues' replication and Boon and Davies' replication are both paywalled with no repository copy, so this entry quotes their abstracts and no figures from either.
misreadings: The football result is almost always told as both sides seeing their own team as cleaner, and that is not what the table says. Dartmouth students saw 4.3 infractions by Dartmouth and 4.4 by Princeton, which is no gap at all, and Princeton students saw 4.2 by their own team, close to the 4.4 the Dartmouth students gave it. One number moved: the 9.8 that Princeton students charged to Dartmouth. Nor did Hastorf and Cantril claim anyone was wrong. They footnote that they are not concerned with guilt, and the referees that day penalised Dartmouth 70 yards to Princeton's 25. The second misreading is that Dearborn and Simon established something. Walsh counted 60 citations to it in the management literature over 1978 to 1987. He then read their published appendix of raw answers and concluded that it is not at all clear their data support their conclusion. Their sales managers named organisational problems, he points out, and their accounting managers named marketing ones. The third is treating the name as a synonym for confirmation bias or motivated reasoning, which have their own entries here. Confirmation bias is about the search for and reading of evidence bearing on a hypothesis. Motivated reasoning is about wanting a conclusion. Selective perception as its founders meant it was a claim about the perceptual act itself, and that is the version Huff and colleagues tested and did not find.
